nameStory: The Flame-shouldered Dart gets its dramatic name from the bright orange or reddish patches that sit like glowing embers on its forewings, resembling shoulder flames when the moth is at rest. The "dart" part refers to this moth's quick, darting flight pattern that's typical of many nocturnal moths in the cutworm family.
description: This is a medium-sized brown moth with distinctive flame-colored shoulder patches that make it stand out from other night-flying moths. Its wingspan reaches about an inch to an inch and a quarter across, making it roughly the size of a large postage stamp. The Flame-shouldered Dart belongs to the cutworm moth family, a group known for their earth-toned colors and nighttime habits. You'll spot adults from spring through early fall, with two generations appearing each year.

idTips.label: Flame-colored shoulder patches
idTips.description: Look for bright orange to reddish patches on the forewings that stand out dramatically against the brown background - these "flames" are the moth's signature feature and appear almost to glow

idTips.label: Brown base coloration
idTips.description: The overall body and wings are various shades of brown, from warm chocolate to grayish-brown, giving it excellent camouflage against tree bark

idTips.label: Medium wingspan
idTips.description: Wings span roughly 1 to 1.25 inches across - about the width of a quarter to slightly larger

idTips.label: Nighttime activity
idTips.description: Most active after dark, often attracted to porch lights and other artificial lighting where they appear suddenly as if from nowhere

idTips.label: Resting position
idTips.description: When at rest during the day, holds wings in a tent-like position over the body, making the flame patches particularly visible from above

habitat: Flame-shouldered Darts are found in a variety of open and semi-open habitats throughout New England, including gardens, fields, meadows, and woodland edges. They're particularly common in areas where their host plants grow - look for them near agricultural areas with beets, clover fields, and areas with chicory and willows. These adaptable moths can be found from sea level to moderate elevations across the region.

seasonality.spring: First generation adults begin emerging in April and May, often attracted to early evening lights. This is when mating occurs and females lay eggs on host plants.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with both first generation completing development and second generation adults emerging. July and August are prime months for spotting adults at lights.
seasonality.fall: Second generation adults continue flying into September, with the last individuals preparing for winter. Larvae from this generation will overwinter in the soil.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not active; larvae spend winter underground in a dormant stage, waiting for spring warmth to resume development.

funFact: This moth was only officially recognized as its own species in 1998 - before then, scientists thought it was the same species as a European moth, meaning countless North American moth watchers had been misidentifying it for over a century!
confusionNotes: The Flame-shouldered Dart can be confused with other brown nocturnal moths, but those distinctive orange shoulder patches are your key - no other common New England moth has quite the same bright "flames" on dark wings. Remember: if you see glowing shoulder patches on a brown moth at your porch light, you've found your flame-bearer.
contextualKnowledge: Until 1998, this moth was incorrectly considered the same species as the European Ochropleura plecta, highlighting how challenging moth identification can be and how new discoveries continue to be made even in well-studied regions like New England.
compareHints: Since this is the only Ochropleura species in New England, compare it to other cutworm moths in the region. Most other brown noctuids lack the distinctive bright orange shoulder patches that make this species so recognizable. The flame-colored markings are much more vivid and well-defined than the subtle markings found on most other members of this large moth family.
